explanation: SET NOCOUNT OFF makes the procedure send row-count messages for its statements in addition to its result sets.
With XACT_ABORT OFF, some run-time errors can abort only the failing statement and leave the explicit transaction active.
@CustomerIdText fixes the customer identifier at N'1', so its later lookup ignores the caller's @CustomerID.
@OrderID starts with the business identifier 1, which remains its value if the later assignment finds no orders.
SELECT * returns every Sales.Orders column, including its nvarchar(max) fields, and makes the result shape depend on the table schema.
No ordering determines which ten OrderIDs are returned.
Sales.Orders.OrderID is the primary key, so DISTINCT cannot remove any rows.
NOLOCK allows the order scan to return uncommitted OrderIDs or to miss or repeat rows during concurrent changes.
YEAR(o.OrderDate) tests a computed value instead of expressing the filter as a range on OrderDate.
The reporting year is fixed at 2016 rather than supplied as a named input.
CustomerID is int, but @CustomerIdText is nvarchar(20). SQL Server implicitly converts the variable to int for the comparison.
The OR combines an all-orders query with a single-customer lookup, which can make one cached plan unsuitable for both cases.
The leading % in N'%urgent%' requires a substring search of Comments rather than a prefix lookup.
ISNULL wraps the indexed CustomerID and obscures a direct equality predicate. The fallback is unnecessary because Orders.CustomerID is NOT NULL.
The ISNULL fallback uses 0 as an undocumented stand-in for a missing customer identifier.
The comparison fixes the requested customer identifier at 1 rather than using @CustomerID.
Adding 0 to the OrderID primary key is redundant and obscures the direct key comparison with @OrderID.
CustomerID <> 1 selects every customer except one and can require reading a large portion of Sales.Orders.
The excluded CustomerID is fixed at 1 without identifying why that customer is exceptional.
TOP (1) has no ordering to determine which order/customer pair is returned.
The CROSS JOIN pairs each order with every customer rather than with its own customer, so the returned pair need not be related.
No ordering determines which matching order line supplies the returned OrderID.
The comma-separated FROM list puts the Orders-to-OrderLines relationship in WHERE, where it is easy to omit when editing filters.
The scalar line count depends on each outer OrderID and can require repeated OrderLines lookups rather than one grouped count.
EXISTS is correlated on o.OrderID. A set-based alternative must join distinct qualifying OrderIDs to avoid duplicating orders with multiple matching lines.
The qualifying line-quantity threshold is fixed at 1 inside the subquery.
ORDER BY repeats the CASE that defines HasComments; ordering by the alias would keep the classification in one place.
ORDER BY 2 identifies OrderDate by position, so reordering the select list can silently change the sort.
OrderDate does not uniquely order the rows. Orders sharing a date can move between pages without OrderID as a tie-breaker.
The branches select different primary-key values and each returns at most one row, so UNION requests unnecessary duplicate elimination.
The first branch fixes OrderID at 1.
The second branch fixes OrderID at 2.
The predicate asks for a count of matching order lines when it only needs to know whether the first match exists.
Every order can assign @OrderID. With no unique filter or ordering, the value retained for later operations is unspecified.
No ordering determines which five OrderIDs are inserted into @OrderIds.
No ordering determines which five OrderIDs populate #ImplicitOrders.
SELECT INTO infers the schema of #ImplicitOrders from the projection rather than declaring its column contract explicitly.
order_cursor is opened for a single FETCH of an arbitrary OrderID; a direct query could obtain the value without cursor setup and cleanup.
The converted @CustomerID is appended to the SQL text, producing different statement text for different customer IDs.
EXEC runs @Sql with the customer identifier embedded in the text instead of binding an int parameter.
The converted @OrderID is concatenated into the query even though the lookup can use a typed parameter.
sys.sp_executesql receives only @Sql; it is given no parameter declaration or bound OrderID value.
#Scratch is explicitly created but never dropped, so it remains allocated until procedure scope ends.
The CATCH returns ERROR_MESSAGE() as a result row but does not signal failure, allowing execution to continue.
The negative-OrderID path uses legacy RAISERROR rather than THROW.
PRINT emits a buffered, unstructured diagnostic rather than a reliably consumable status or log entry.
The order lookup fixes CustomerID at 1 despite the available @CustomerID parameter.
The OrderDate cutoff '20160101' is embedded in the predicate without a name or parameter explaining its significance.
Without an explicit conversion style, '01/02/2016' can mean January 2 or February 1 depending on the session date format.
TOP (1) has no ordering to determine which invoice-matched order is returned.
COALESCE(o.CustomerID, 0) wraps the Orders join key even though it is NOT NULL; the indexed column can be compared directly.
COALESCE(i.CustomerID, 0) independently wraps the Invoices join key, which is also indexed and NOT NULL.
No ordering determines which OrderID is selected from the self-join.
Joining Orders to itself on its primary key matches each row only to itself and supplies no additional information.
Sorting orders by the nvarchar(max) Comments column can require expensive text comparisons and substantial sort memory.
SUM(ol.Quantity) reads quantities across all of Sales.OrderLines because no order or reporting range restricts the total.
OrderID > 0 depends only on the grouping key and can be expressed in WHERE rather than as a group filter.
The unfiltered COUNT(*) requires a count of all rows in Sales.Orders.
COUNT(*) without GROUP BY returns exactly one row, so ordering by OrderCount cannot change the result.
MERGE is used solely for a matched update; an ordinary keyed UPDATE can express the operation without MERGE-specific complexity.
The matched action assigns target.Comments to itself, potentially taking update locks and firing triggers without changing the value.
The keyed UPDATE writes Comments back to itself and can incur write-side effects without changing the order.
Quantity is not an order-line key. The DELETE removes every line with quantity -1, regardless of which order it belongs to.
The unexplained quantity value -1 determines which order lines are deleted.
WAITFOR DELAY keeps the request waiting for one second before the procedure can continue.
The transaction begins outside TRY/CATCH, so there is no error-handling path if execution fails before its ROLLBACK.
The supplied Sales.Orders definition has no IDENTITY column, so enabling IDENTITY_INSERT for it fails when reached.
EXEC sp_who leaves the system procedure's schema implicit rather than naming sys.sp_who.
SET ROWCOUNT 1 is not reset inside the procedure. Later queries and writes, including the customer copy, can stop after one row.
The VALUES insert relies on the declared order of CategoryID and CategoryName in #DemoCategories.
The inserted category gets the fixed identifier 99 regardless of the supplied category name.
The four selected customer fields map to #DemoCustomers by position because the INSERT names no target columns.
Prepending '%' to @CustomerName prevents a prefix seek on the CustomerName index.
@CustomerName is concatenated inside a quoted SQL literal. Caller input can change the executed statement rather than remain a search value.
The call names sp_executesql without its sys schema qualifier.
sp_executesql receives only the assembled text; it does not bind the customer search pattern as a parameter.
Every row in #DemoCustomers qualifies for the update. The active ROWCOUNT limit restricts how many can change, not which customer is intended.
The update assigns the fixed CustomerCategoryID 1 rather than a supplied or looked-up category identifier.
The WHERE predicate rejects NULL-extended order rows, so the LEFT JOIN does not preserve customers without a qualifying order.
The qualifying-order cutoff '2016-01-01' is fixed in the predicate without a named business meaning.
DeliveryMethodID = NULL does not test for a missing value. It cannot select a row, and DeliveryMethodID is declared NOT NULL.
dbo.GetCustomerType(CustomerID) can execute separately for each customer unless SQL Server can inline the scalar function.
An error before COMMIT can leave the transaction active or uncommittable, but the CATCH does not check transaction state or roll it back.
The CATCH only selects ERROR_MESSAGE(), so a failed delete or commit is not propagated to the caller as a failure.
INDEX = 1 forces the clustered index on Sales.Customers and prevents the optimizer from choosing the CustomerName index for the LIKE predicate.
Three nested derived tables merely pass CustomerID outward. One SELECT from Sales.Customers can return the same filtered result.
LIKE '%A%' searches anywhere in CustomerName, so the name index cannot seek to a matching prefix.
SELECT * exposes every column returned by dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti and couples the result shape to the function definition.

If dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti is a multi-statement TVF as its name suggests, it materializes its result without column statistics. Its definition is needed to confirm whether an inline query can replace it.
